title: Communication Skills–II
short: Methods, feedback, barriers, 7 Cs and basic writing skills.
lede: The complete study cycle for Unit 1: methods of communication, the cycle with feedback, barriers, the 7 Cs and basic writing skills — book-style Q&A with hidden answers.
lens: **2 marks inside the 10-mark Part A.** Mostly MCQ plus one short written answer.
Learn the **7-step cycle**, the **7 Cs** and one example each of verbal / non-verbal / visual.
concepts: **1. Communication** is the transfer of information, ideas or feelings between a sender and a receiver through a medium, with **feedback** completing the loop.
**2. Communication cycle (draw this in a 2-marker):** Sender → Encoding → Message → Channel → Decoding → Receiver → Feedback.
**3. Feedback** is the receiver's response. Good feedback is **descriptive, specific, timely and constructive**. It is called the lifeline because it confirms understanding and corrects errors early.
**4. Barriers:** physical (noise, distance), linguistic (jargon, another language), cultural (gesture meanings), emotional (anger), perceptual, organisational, interpersonal.
**5. 7 Cs of effective communication:** Clear, Concise, Concrete, Correct, Coherent, Complete, Courteous.

**6. Basic writing skills.** A **sentence** has a subject and a predicate. A **phrase** is a group of words without a finite verb. Kinds of sentences: declarative, interrogative, imperative, exclamatory. Parts of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, interjection, article. **Articles:** a / an / the. A paragraph starts with a **topic sentence**, then supporting details, then a close.
**7. Paralanguage** is *how* the voice sounds — tone, pitch, speed, pauses. Book fact often quoted: words 7%, voice 38%, body 55%.
formulas: 7 Cs: Clear · Concise · Concrete · Correct · Coherent · Complete · Courteous
tricks: - 7 Cs mnemonic: **Can Cows Chew Cold Corn Cob Candy?**
- Cycle order: **SEMC DRF** — Sender, Encoding, Message, Channel, Decoding, Receiver, Feedback.
- Non-verbal is the **easiest** method — it needs no language or literacy.
mistakes: - Writing only verbal/non-verbal and skipping the **oral vs written** split.
- Forgetting an **example** in a 2-marker — the example carries half the marks.

qa.q: Enlist the different methods of communication.
qa.a: ** (1) Verbal** — oral (speech, phone, meeting) + written (letter, email, report). **(2) Non-verbal** — expressions, gestures, posture, eye contact, tone. **(3) Visual** — charts, maps, signals, posters, videos.

qa.q: Which is the easiest method of communication and why?
qa.a: **Non-verbal** is the easiest — it needs no language or literacy. Gestures, expressions and tone are understood naturally and work across languages.

qa.q: What is feedback? Why is it called the lifeline of communication?
qa.a: Feedback is the receiver's response flowing back to the sender. It is the lifeline because it (1) confirms the message was understood and (2) corrects errors early — completing the two-way loop.

qa.q: Explain any two Cs of effective communication with examples.
qa.a: (1) **Clear** — simple, exact message (“Submit the file by Friday 5 pm”). (2) **Courteous** — polite words (“please”, “thank you”, “sorry for the delay”).

qa.q: Name any four barriers to effective communication.
qa.a: Physical barriers such as noise or distance; language barriers such as jargon or an unfamiliar accent; psychological barriers such as anger, fear or prejudice; and cultural barriers, where the same word or gesture means different things. Poor listening and the absence of feedback make all of them worse.

qa.q: Riya messages her team “do it soon”. Identify the violated C and rewrite the message correctly.
qa.a: Violates **Clear** (vague, no deadline) and **Complete** (no what/when). Rewrite: “Please submit the sales sheet by Friday 5 pm on email.” — now clear, complete and courteous.

qa.q: A team leader’s juniors look confused by his technical jargon. What two steps should he take?
qa.a: (1) Replace jargon with simple words and show a chart (linguistic barrier). (2) Pause, ask “any doubts?”, and paraphrase replies (feedback + active listening).

qa.q: What are the 7 Cs of effective communication? Explain any three.
a: The seven Cs are clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete and courteous.
Clear: say what you mean in words the listener understands, and avoid jargon.
Concise: use only as many words as the message needs, so the point is not lost.
Complete: give all the facts the receiver needs, including who, what, when and where, so that no further questions are needed.

qa.q: Discuss in detail the verbal method of communication.
a: Verbal = communication using **words**, in two forms.
**Oral** (speech, phone, meeting): fast, instant feedback; no permanent record.
**Written** (letter, email, report): permanent proof, re-readable, formal; slower, needs literacy.
Use oral for urgent/personal matters, written when a record is needed.

qa.q: Explain any four barriers to communication with one example and one measure each.
a: (1) **Physical** — class noise → quiet room, working mic.
(2) **Linguistic** — French manual → simple words + visuals.
(3) **Cultural** — a thumbs-up is rude in some places → learn customs.
(4) **Emotional** — anger blocks listening → stay calm, choose the right time.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Amit presents with zero eye contact, 40 text-packed slides in 10 minutes, and says “no questions, I am getting late”. The manager understands nothing.

(a) Identify four communication mistakes.
(b) Suggest four fixes.
a: (a) No eye contact (poor non-verbal) • overloaded slides (not concise) • too fast (not clear) • no questions (blocks feedback).
(b) Eye contact + open posture • max 10 slides, one idea each • slow, clear speech • invite questions and summarise.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

For the school fest, Class X puts up posters at shops, announces on a loudspeaker, and the principal sends a written notice to parents.

(a) Name the three methods used.
(b) Why is combining them better than one?
a: (a) Posters = **visual**; loudspeaker = **oral/verbal**; notice = **written**.
(b) Visual attracts, oral spreads fast, written is proof — together they cover more audiences with both speed and a record.

mcq.q: Which part of communication converts an idea into words or signs? (a) Receiving (b) Encoding (c) Decoding (d) Feedback
mcq.a: **(b) Encoding.** Encoding prepares the sender's idea as a message; decoding interprets it.

mcq.q: A loud generator prevents a worker from hearing instructions. The barrier is: (a) linguistic (b) cultural (c) physical (d) emotional
mcq.a: **(c) Physical** — environmental noise blocks the message.

mcq.q: Which of the 7 Cs means “to the point, no extra words”? (a) Clear (b) Concise (c) Concrete (d) Courteous
mcq.a: **(b) Concise.**

mcq.q: “An honest boy” takes which article? (a) a (b) an (c) the (d) no article
mcq.a: **(b) an** — use *an* before a vowel **sound**; h is silent in honest.

mcq.q: A student's puzzled expression after an explanation is: (a) written encoding (b) non-verbal feedback (c) a channel (d) a language rule
mcq.a: **(b) Non-verbal feedback.**

mcq.q: Which sentence is complete? (a) Do that work. (b) The form is important. (c) Submit the signed form to Room 4 by Friday noon. (d) Submit it soon.
mcq.a: **(c)** — task, place and deadline are all present.

mcq.q: Paralanguage refers to: (a) body posture only (b) charts and maps (c) tone, pitch and speed of voice (d) grammar rules
mcq.a: **(c) Tone, pitch and speed of voice.**

mcq.q: The easiest method of communication is: (a) written (b) oral (c) non-verbal (d) email
mcq.a: **(c) Non-verbal** — needs no literacy.

mcq.q: The communication process is complete only when: (a) the receiver gives feedback  (b) the message is written  (c) the sender speaks  (d) the channel is chosen
mcq.a: **(a) the receiver gives feedback.** Feedback tells the sender whether the message was understood.

mcq.q: Which method of communication carries no body language or tone of voice? (a) written communication  (b) face-to-face talk  (c) video call  (d) group discussion
mcq.a: **(a) written communication.** That is why written messages must be especially clear.

trend: One 2-mark on methods, 7 Cs or feedback, plus 1-mark MCQs on barriers and articles.
onepager: - Cycle: Sender → Encoding → Message → Channel → Decoding → Receiver → Feedback.
- 7 Cs: Clear Concise Concrete Correct Coherent Complete Courteous.
- Good feedback: descriptive, specific, timely, constructive.
task: Write a formal email to the principal requesting one day's leave. Subject, greeting, 3-line body, sign-off — that is written communication plus courtesy.

title: Self-Management Skills–II
short: Stress, self-awareness, self-motivation, self-regulation, time and SMART goals.
lede: The highest-scoring employability unit. Lists plus one workplace example cover almost every question.
lens: **3 marks.** Stress symptoms, SMART goals and time-management steps are the usual asks.
Always add a **workplace example** — a data-entry operator under a deadline is enough.
concepts: **1. Self-management** is the ability to control one's emotions, thoughts and behaviour and to work towards goals without constant supervision.

**2. Stress** is the body's response to pressure. **Eustress** is positive (a deadline that focuses you); **distress** is harmful. Symptoms: headache, fast heartbeat, irritability, poor sleep, missed errors.
**3. Stress management:** deep breathing, short breaks, exercise, talking to someone, breaking work into chunks, saying no to extra load, sleep and a hobby.
**4. Self-awareness** is knowing your strengths, weaknesses, values and emotions. Tools: SWOT, feedback from others, a journal.
**5. Self-motivation** is working without being pushed. Intrinsic (interest, pride) lasts longer than extrinsic (marks, money).
**6. Self-regulation** is managing impulses — staying calm, delaying gratification, following rules.
**7. Time management:** list tasks, set priorities (urgent/important), use a timetable, avoid multitasking, finish one chunk, review at the end of the day.
**8. SMART goals:** Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic/Relevant, Time-bound. “Type 30 invoices without error by 5 pm Friday” is SMART; “do better” is not.
tricks: - Urgent vs important: exam tomorrow is both; scrolling is neither.
mistakes: - Writing SMART expansions in the wrong order.
- Treating all stress as bad — eustress is useful.

qa.q: What is self-management? Give two of its benefits.
qa.a: Controlling one's emotions, thoughts and behaviour to reach goals. Benefits: better work quality, less stress, meeting deadlines, less need for supervision.

qa.q: Differentiate eustress and distress with one example each.
qa.a: **Eustress** is helpful pressure — a timed practical that makes you focus. **Distress** is harmful — so much overtime that errors increase and sleep is lost.

qa.q: Distinguish between stress and a stressor.
qa.a: Stress is the way the body and mind react to pressure, while a stressor is the event or situation that triggers it. An examination, a deadline, a family problem or a noisy workplace can each be a stressor; the resulting worry, headache or loss of sleep is the stress.

qa.q: Meera has three tasks: a 5 pm file, a messy desk, and a social-media reel. Using urgent/important, what should she do first and why?
qa.a: The 5 pm file is urgent and important — do it first. The desk is important but not urgent — schedule it. The reel is neither — drop it until the file is in.

qa.q: Riya is revising “Self-Management Skills–II” (Stress, self-awareness, self-motivation, self-regulation, time and SMART goals.). A classmate lost marks by doing this: Writing SMART expansions in the wrong order. Apply the correct method and rewrite the scoring answer.
a: Correct method: SMART → Specific Measurable Achievable Realistic Time-bound.
Why the mistake costs marks: Writing SMART expansions in the wrong order.
Write the definition or formula first, then the working or example.

qa.q: Suggest three ways of managing stress and building self-motivation.
a: Plan the day, break big tasks into small ones and do the hardest first, so that the work never feels endless.
Look after the body: sleep enough, exercise, breathe deeply and eat regularly, because a tired body exaggerates every problem.
Set specific goals, track them, reward yourself when a goal is met, and talk to someone you trust instead of keeping worries inside.

qa.q: Explain SMART goals with a data-entry example.
qa.a: Specific (which file), Measurable (how many records), Achievable (within skill), Realistic (hours available), Time-bound (by 5 pm). Example: “Enter 80 customer rows in Calc with zero blanks by 4 pm today.”

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Ravi’s hands shake before every practical, he skips breakfast and then makes typing errors.

(a) Name the type of stress.
(b) List four management steps.
(c) Write one SMART goal for his next practical.
a: (a) Distress — it is harming performance.
(b) Breakfast, 4–7 breathing, a 5-minute practice file, a checklist, sleep 7 hours.
(c) “Complete the Base table of 10 records with primary key set, in 25 minutes, with zero errors, on Friday.”

title: ICT Skills–II
short: Operating system, files and folders, and basic care of a computer.
lede: One mark, almost all MCQ. File, folder, recycle bin and care-of-computer lists are enough.
lens: **1 mark.** Definitions and “which of the following” items.
Know **OS functions**, **file vs folder**, and **three care tips**.
concepts: **1. ICT** is Information and Communication Technology — hardware, software and networks used to create, store and share information.

**2. Operating system (OS)** is system software that manages hardware and lets you run programs. Examples: Windows, Linux, macOS, Android. Functions: start the computer, manage files, memory, devices and security, provide a user interface.
**3. File** = a named collection of data (report.odt). **Folder** = a container for files and other folders. Use short, meaningful names and extensions (.odt, .ods, .odb, .jpg).
**4. Care of computer:** keep it dust-free, don't eat or drink near it, use a surge protector, shut down properly, update antivirus, don't install unknown software, backup important files.
**5. Maintenance:** disk cleanup, defragment (HDD), update OS, scan for malware, keep vents clear so the machine does not overheat.
tricks: - File has an **extension**; a folder does not need one.
- OS = the **manager** of the machine, not an application like Writer.
mistakes: - Saving everything on the Desktop with names like `final2(1).odt`.

qa.q: What is an operating system? Give two examples.
qa.a: System software that manages hardware and runs programs. Examples: Windows, Linux, Android.

qa.q: Differentiate a file and a folder with one example each.
qa.a: A **file** stores data (`marks.ods`). A **folder** stores files and other folders (`Class10/IT/`).

qa.q: What is an operating system? Name two examples.
qa.a: An operating system is the system software that manages the computer's memory, processor, disks and devices and lets the user run application programs. Examples are Windows, Linux, macOS and Android.

qa.q: Amit eats chips over the keyboard and never shuts the PC down. List three risks and three care steps.
qa.a: Risks: crumbs jam keys, oil damage, overheating, data loss. Care: no food/drink, proper shutdown, dust-free vents, surge protector, backups.

qa.q: Riya is revising “ICT Skills–II” (Operating system, files and folders, and basic care of a computer.). A classmate lost marks by doing this: Calling Writer an operating system. Apply the correct method and rewrite the scoring answer.
a: Correct method: File has an extension; a folder does not need one.
Why the mistake costs marks: Calling Writer an operating system.
Write the definition or formula first, then the working or example.

qa.q: How would you organise files and folders so that your work is always easy to find?
a: Make one folder for each subject or project, and inside it one folder per term or per type of work.
Give every file a short, descriptive name with the date, such as maths_notes_2026-08-12.
Keep the folder tree shallow — no more than two or three levels — and delete or archive old versions.
Keep a backup copy on an external drive or in the cloud, and run an antivirus scan on anything you download.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Meera’s project file vanished after a power cut. She had saved only on the Desktop as `aaa.odt`.

(a) Two file-management mistakes.
(b) Two care/maintenance steps that would have helped.
a: (a) No backup; a meaningless file name; Desktop-only copy.
(b) Surge protector / UPS; Save As into a named folder; weekly backup on a pen drive or cloud.

title: Entrepreneurial Skills–II
short: Who an entrepreneur is, qualities, functions, myths and role in society.
lede: Definition plus four qualities plus one myth — that is the whole 3-mark answer.
lens: **3 marks.** Qualities of an entrepreneur and “role in society” rotate.
Always add a **small Indian example** (a local bakery, a tutoring app).
concepts: **1. Entrepreneur** — a person who spots a need, takes a risk, organises resources and starts a business to earn profit and create value.
**2. Entrepreneurship** is the process of creating and running that venture.
**3. Qualities:** initiative, risk-taking, creativity, perseverance, self-confidence, leadership, problem-solving, honesty, hard work.
**4. Functions:** identify opportunity, arrange land/labour/capital, hire and lead, take decisions, bear risk, innovate, market the product.

**5. Myths:** “entrepreneurs are born, not made”; “you need a huge amount of money”; “it is only for the highly educated”; “failure means the person is useless”. All false — skills can be learned, many start small, failure is data.
**6. Role in society:** jobs, new products, use of local resources, wealth, solving local problems (waste, transport, tuition).
**7. Types (brief):** small business, scalable start-up, social entrepreneur (profit is not the only aim).
tricks: - Quality vs function: quality is a **trait** (perseverance); function is a **job** (arrange capital).
- Myth answers always start with **False**, then the correction.
mistakes: - Calling every shopkeeper an entrepreneur without the risk/innovation idea.

qa.q: Who is an entrepreneur? Give two qualities.
qa.a: A person who spots a need, takes a risk and organises resources to start a venture. Qualities: initiative and perseverance (or creativity, self-confidence).

qa.q: State two myths about entrepreneurship and correct them.
qa.a: (1) “Born, not made” — skills can be learned. (2) “Needs huge capital” — many start with a small idea and grow.

qa.q: List any four qualities an entrepreneur needs.
qa.a: Self-confidence, the willingness to take calculated risks, initiative and perseverance, the ability to plan and organise, and the readiness to learn from failure and try again.

qa.q: Neha notices students waiting 40 minutes for a shared printer. She starts a paid print-and-bind desk. Which entrepreneurial qualities is she using?
qa.a: Opportunity-spotting, initiative, risk-taking (she invests in a printer), problem-solving and customer focus.

qa.q: Riya is revising “Entrepreneurial Skills–II” (Who an entrepreneur is, qualities, functions, myths and role in society.). A classmate lost marks by doing this: Calling every shopkeeper an entrepreneur without the risk/innovation idea. Apply the correct method and rewrite the scoring answer.
a: Correct method: Quality vs function: quality is a trait (perseverance); function is a job (arrange capital).
Why the mistake costs marks: Calling every shopkeeper an entrepreneur without the risk/innovation idea.
Write the definition or formula first, then the working or example.

qa.q: What functions does an entrepreneur perform in running an enterprise?
a: Spotting an opportunity and turning it into a product or service people will pay for.
Arranging the money, buying raw materials, machines and premises, and hiring and training workers.
Organising production, keeping accounts and marketing the product.
Bearing the risk of loss, and taking the decisions that keep the enterprise alive.

qa.q: Explain four functions of an entrepreneur with a bakery example.
qa.a: Identify demand for fresh bread; arrange shop, oven and staff; take the risk of unsold stock; market via samples and a board; keep accounts. Each function maps to one quality: opportunity-spotting, organising, risk-taking, selling.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

(c) State two roles of entrepreneurship in society.
a: (a) Myth of huge capital / only the highly educated.
(b) A tiffin service from a home kitchen; a tuition class in a garage.
(c) Jobs, new products, local resources used, local problems solved.

mcq.q: A person who starts a business, organises it and bears its risks is a/an: (a) entrepreneur  (b) manager  (c) employee  (d) customer
mcq.a: **(a) entrepreneur.** A manager runs someone else's business for a salary.

mcq.q: Which of these is a myth about entrepreneurs? (a) they are born, not made  (b) they take risks  (c) they work hard  (d) they need capital
mcq.a: **(a) they are born, not made.** Entrepreneurial skills such as planning, selling and record-keeping can be learned.

title: Green Skills–II
short: Sustainable development, green economy and green jobs.
lede: One-mark unit. Definition of sustainable development plus two green practices.
lens: **1 mark.** Sustainable development definition is the banker.
Add **reduce, reuse, recycle** and one green job.
concepts: **1. Environment** = the surroundings in which we live — air, water, land, plants, animals and humans.
**2. Sustainable development** meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
**3. Green economy** is low-carbon, resource-efficient and socially inclusive. Growth does not destroy the environment.
**4. Green skills** are the knowledge and attitudes needed for a sustainable society — saving energy, waste segregation, water conservation, green design.
**5. Green jobs:** solar technician, waste-segregation worker, organic farmer, green-building auditor, bicycle mechanic.
**6. Everyday practices:** switch off unused devices, use both sides of paper, carry a bottle, segregate dry/wet waste, plant trees, use public transport.
tricks: - Sustainable development = **present + future**, not only “planting trees”.
- 3 Rs: Reduce first (best), then Reuse, then Recycle.
mistakes: - Defining sustainable development as “using no resources”. It is **wise use**, not zero use.
- Mixing green skills with ICT skills.

qa.q: Define sustainable development.
qa.a: Development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

qa.q: What are green skills? Give two examples.
qa.a: Skills that help a person live and work in an environmentally friendly way. Examples: waste segregation, saving electricity, water conservation.

qa.q: What is sustainable development?
qa.a: It is development that meets the needs of the present without reducing the ability of future generations to meet their own needs — using resources carefully, keeping pollution low and protecting ecosystems while the economy grows.

qa.q: A computer lab leaves 20 PCs on overnight. Suggest three green practices and one green skill the lab assistant needs.
qa.a: Shut down PCs, use sleep mode, switch off AC/lights, enable duplex printing. Skill: energy-conservation habit / e-waste handling.

qa.q: Riya is revising “Green Skills–II” (Sustainable development, green economy and green jobs.). A classmate lost marks by doing this: Defining sustainable development as “using no resources”. It is wise use, not zero use. Apply the correct method and rewrite the scoring answer.
a: Correct method: Sustainable development = present + future, not only “planting trees”.
Why the mistake costs marks: Defining sustainable development as “using no resources”. It is wise use, not zero use.
Write the definition or formula first, then the working or example.

qa.q: Give three examples of green jobs and explain what makes a job green.
a: Installing and maintaining solar panels, managing recycling and composting, organic farming, water harvesting and energy auditing are all green jobs.
A job is green when it reduces the use of energy or raw materials, cuts greenhouse-gas emissions and waste, and protects or restores ecosystems.
It should also provide decent work and income, because a green economy is meant to improve human well-being as well as the environment.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

A factory dumps dye in a river but pays workers well.

(a) Is this sustainable development? Why?
(b) Name two green-economy changes.
(c) One green job this town could create.
a: (a) No — present wages at the cost of future water and health.
(b) Treat effluent, switch to safer dye, reuse water.
(c) Water-treatment operator or waste-segregation worker.

mcq.q: Leaving a PC on overnight mainly wastes: (a) paper (b) electricity (c) toner only (d) nothing

mcq.q: The most exam-ready way to revise “Green Skills–II” is: (a) read the heading only  (b) learn the key idea plus one example  (c) skip written practice  (d) memorise a random extra topic

mcq.q: A green economy is one that: (a) improves human well-being while reducing environmental risks  (b) produces the most goods  (c) bans all industry  (d) depends only on coal
mcq.a: **(a) improves human well-being while reducing environmental risks.** It is low-carbon and resource-efficient.

mcq.q: Which of these is a green skill? (a) segregating waste at source  (b) leaving taps running  (c) burning dry leaves  (d) using a plastic bag every day
mcq.a: **(a) segregating waste at source.** It makes recycling possible and cuts the load on landfills.
